channel.title: Void Weekly: The Argument
channel.description: The Sunday edition of Void News, read by three voices. The week's cover story, then the two columnists who disagree about it, reading their own published words at each other across a held pause. Then what each of them leaves out, the week's coverage measured, and the question it leaves open. No ads. No paywall.

item.title: Issue #26: Arctic Sovereignty, Contested Control — WEEKLY Evening Brief
item.description:
On Friday, September 18, the United States, Denmark, and Greenland announced an agreement for a US military presence on Greenland, a development that followed months of diplomatic tension. President Donald Trump, however, immediately asserted Washington would have "permanent control" over the island's security, a claim Denmark and Greenland quickly countered by affirming their sovereignty. The agreement, disclosed late Friday, stipulated that US adversaries could not establish bases or maintain a military presence in Greenland. It further prohibited sensitive investments without Washington's express written approval. Yet, the extent of the US military presence and whether formal power over foreign policy and resources would be ceded remained undisclosed.
This agreement emerged from a period of uncertainty, triggered by President Trump's earlier threats to seize control of Greenland. Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump had repeatedly insisted Washington needed to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and sparking pushback from the alliance. Denmark and Greenland had consistently maintained that Washington must respect the sovereignty of the Danish kingdom and accept that Greenland was not for sale.
Danish Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen stated on Saturday, September 19, that the coming week could prove productive, expressing hope that a period of uncertainty would yield a binding agreement. Rasmussen added that the agreement strengthened security in the Arctic and North Atlantic, thereby bolstering shared security within NATO and Europe, while respecting the Danish Kingdom's "red lines." Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen described the deal as recognizing the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the Greenlandic people's right to self-determination.
On Truth Social late Friday, President Trump declared the United States would "FOREVER have the complete ability to do what is necessary in Greenland" to secure its own and US security. He termed it an "'Infinite Life' Agreement" with no end, stating Washington would immediately begin building a large military presence. This assertion stood in contrast to the statements from Copenhagen and Nuuk, which emphasized the deal's respect for Greenlandic self-determination and Danish sovereignty.
International outlets reflected this divergence in emphasis. Some, including The Jerusalem Post and Reuters, led with Denmark and Greenland's focus on sovereignty. Others, such as The Straits Times and Dawn, highlighted Trump's claim of "permanent control." Reuters and other international sources detailed the lack of public information regarding the degree of US military presence or formal power ceded, while some outlets focused more on the political statements from leaders. Several international sources, including The Straits Times and Channel News Asia, included Rasmussen's social media statements about the deal ending uncertainty and respecting "red lines."
By Saturday, September 19, experts began to weigh in, with some suggesting Denmark had achieved a favorable outcome in the deal with President Trump. Leaders from Denmark and Greenland expressed cautious optimism, hoping the agreement, expected to be signed during the UN General Assembly next week, would resolve the months of uncertainty. The agreement, as presented by Denmark and Greenland, aimed to end the diplomatic friction that had characterized the relationship since Trump's renewed interest in the island.
